doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Driving to Chicago to persuade Teddy Wilson to come to New York
summary: Hammond financed the trip, Carter drove with George Rich, and they talked a shy Wilson into coming.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: But to continue on the John Hammond thing, when I went—and this is jumping ahead, of course—when I did go to Europe . . . was it when I . . . no, it wasn’t; it was just, oh, just some months later when I was putting my band together, and I think by that time I had an upcoming engagement. I mentioned to him that I had heard this pianist and I would like to get him to come to New York. I don’t know what the conditions were that . . . I don’t know. We couldn’t talk him into coming, you know, through correspondence or phone or whatever. So I went to Chicago to meet him and talk with him, and this trip was financed by Hammond to the tune of, I think, $150, or $160, to hit the correct figure. I drove there with a friend of mine who had just bought a new Cadillac, a very dear and close friend, a most generous man, named . . . hmm, Jesus . . . George Rich. I’m saying all of this to say what?
About getting Teddy Wilson. So we did talk to Teddy, and we convinced him to come to New York, which he did shortly thereafter.
Had you spoken to him when you saw him in Woonsocket?
Oh yes, I met him, you know.
You got to meet him and . . .
Sure, yeah, got to meet him, yeah.
What did he seem like personally to you? What sort of a . . .
Quiet, intelligent, a little unassuming, even a wee bit shy.
Do you think that may have been the reason he needed personal coaxing to get him to . . .

Yeah. Yeah, I think he didn’t want to leave Chicago. That was his home base at the time, although he was originally from Tuskegee, Alabama, I believe. But he was doing well in Chicago and probably didn’t realize what would lay ahead in New York, you know.
